unit_label: CB Module B unit 3: financial inclusion and development (courseware unit 6)

facts.statement: Meaning, objectives and impediments (courseware): the objectives of financial inclusion are (a) the broadening of financial services to those people and enterprises who do not have access to the financial services sector; (b) the deepening of financial services for those who have minimal financial services; and (c) greater financial literacy and consumer protection so that those who are offered financial products can make appropriate choices. Financial inclusion places financial products in the hands of larger sections of society, enabling them to partake in the growth and prosperity of the country and strengthening the transmission of monetary policy. Financial inclusion in the sense of access to the formal financial system for basic financial services at a reasonable cost is now positioned as a policy objective in more than 60 countries; it is central to the UN 2030 Sustainable Development Goals and the G 20 Action Plan on the 2030 Agenda; the UN Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) reports evidence of financial inclusion contributing to a stable financial system (financially included economic agents appear to be able to ride out interest rate cycles pro-cyclically instead of being impacted counter-cyclically). In India the main objective of pursuing financial inclusion is widespread relevance in the wake of the observation that despite witnessing growth and economic development since independence, several sections of society do not have access to the fruits of financial development. The major impediments: (a) difficulty in servicing these sections of the population as they may be remotely placed, (b) it may not be possible to serve them with ease and profitability and (c) lack of necessary institutional arrangements in terms of providing financial incentives to those that drive the financial inclusion process. Dr Raghuram Rajan characterised the impediments by the acronym IIT: Information, Incentives and Transaction Costs. The excluded may live in remote areas or belong to communities that undertake economic activity informally and do not maintain records or have signed contracts or documentation; they often do not own property or have regular established sources of income, so a banker has difficulty getting sufficient information to offer financial products (information); incentives: lenders are easily avoided if the lender thinks he will not be repaid; when the local legal system does not enforce repayment quickly or cheaply and the borrower does not have any collateral to pledge, the lender might believe that he will find it difficult to get repaid; transaction costs: the fixed costs in transacting are relatively high; it takes as much time helping a client fill out the forms and to provide the necessary documentation if he is applying for a loan for Rs 10,000 to help another one to borrow Rs 10 lakh.

Policy interventions: mandates and subventions (courseware): an important policy decision could be to mandate banks allocate a certain fraction of their loans to the priority sector and that they open 25 per cent of their branches in unbanked areas; there are also interest subventions that are made available for loans to specific sectors; furthermore banks have been urged to open bank accounts for all under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), while today they have to make loans to small businesses under the Mudra Scheme. Because there are positive social benefits to financial inclusion that are not captured by the service provider (what economists call externalities), such mandates are reasonable from a societal perspective; for instance, the higher familial and community status a farm worker gets from starting her own poultry farm and contributing to the family income may outweigh the costs the bank incurs on making the loan. In a similar vein there are network benefits from universal access: direct transfer of benefits is easier when a vast majority of beneficiaries have a bank account, and the institutions themselves will be used heavily when account transfers are made easier through mobile phones via the Unified Payments Interface (UPI); mandated account opening essentially creates the universal network with its associated positive network externalities. There are, however, several risks emanating from mandates: the first is that there is no market test of usefulness and these may not be possible; some vested interests may benefit from specific mandates and push for their perpetuation long after they have ceased being useful; bankers themselves may be tempted to target the most accessible and least risky in the eligible category and even mislabelling normal activity so that it fits in the eligible list; finally, some mandates fall primarily on the public sector banks, so competition reduces their profitability. The RBI has tried to make mandates more effective: the list of sectors eligible for priority sector treatment has been revised, with an emphasis on targeting the truly excluded: the share of adjusted net bank credit (ANBC) that has to go to small and marginal farmers (including sharecroppers) was set at 8 per cent for March 2017 and that for micro enterprises at 7.5 per cent; the scope for banks to meet priority sector norms without lending to the truly excluded has been reduced: for example, large loans to firms producing agricultural products no longer qualify; banks are now required to meet their targets at the end of every quarter, rather than at the end of the year, which reduces the scope for window-dressing; Priority Sector Lending Certificates allow a lender to sell any over-achievement in particular categories to others who are deficient, thus encouraging those who have a better capacity to make such loans to do so. Mandates are not costless: rather than forcing banks to recover costs by overcharging ordinary customers, or by demanding recapitalisation by the government, better to bring the costs into the open by paying for the mandate wherever possible; for instance accounts or cash machines opened in remote areas could attract a fixed subsidy, which would be paid to anyone who delivers them; the RBI explicitly subsidises cash recyclers set up in underserved areas.

Institutional structure, digital technology and payments (courseware): the moneylender is particularly effective because he knows the neighbourhood; a large national bank with a local branch manager typically has an all-India exam recruit from a different state and not intimately familiar with the local people; branch managers in large banks with bureaucratic centralised processes find it hard to provide effective service. Local financial institutions with local control and staffed by knowledgeable local people could be more effective at providing financial services to the excluded; HDFC Bank, for example, has been very successful growing its loan portfolio in Kashmir by recruiting local youth as loan officers; micro finance institutions combine local knowledge with stronger incentives for repayment through peer pressure and frequent collection; this was the rationale for local area banks, regional rural banks and the strong feature in the co-operative movement. However micro finance institutions do not have access to low-cost deposit financing; local area banks could not expand out of their local area, exposing them to geographical concentration risks; regional rural banks agitated for parity in salary structures with parent scheduled commercial banks and found that their costs are not optimally suited for the clientele they need to serve; some co-operative banks, on par with any universal bank, but far too many suffer from governance problems; the RBI has been engaged in bringing stronger governance to urban co-operative banks but split supervision with state authorities limits what it can do. An alternative institutional avenue was created: the small finance bank, where small refers to the kind of customer the bank deals with, not its size: the small finance bank is intended to be below 25 lakhs; thus 75 per cent of the loans must be to priority sector and 50 per cent of the loan portfolio loans below Rs 25 lakh. Credit information bureaus can help ease the information problem: where an individual knows that a default will limit their credit rating and cut off future access to credit, they have strong incentives to make timely payments; in rural India we need to expand the reach of credit bureaus, including by bringing borrowing under Self Help Groups into their ambit; use of Aadhaar can help in identifying individuals; the Credit Information Bureau of India Limited (CIBIL) provides individuals with one free credit report a year; a proposal by the government for small businesses is Udhyog Aadhaar numbers, which are unique IDs tied to the entity as well as the promoter; land records: the digitisation of land records, accompanied by a guarantee of certificates of full ownership by the state government, as proposed in Rajasthan, will ease the use of land as collateral against which funds can be borrowed; MSMEs are squeezed by large buyers who pay after long delays; Trade-Receivables Discounting Systems (TReDS) platforms licensed by the RBI help MSME sell their claim on the large buyer in the market. Focus on payment and settlement systems vs focus on extension of credit: for decades the focus has been on expanding remunerative savings vehicles, easing payments and remittances, or providing insurance against crop failures; now the Government and RBI are trying to expand inclusion by encouraging working with the poorest to put aside money as savings, allowing credit to follow rather than the other way; many successful organisations working with the poorest, such as self-help groups, take small savings and the discipline instilled by regular savings helps the customer to handle repayment better; easy payments and cash out will make formal savings more attractive: a villager who puts money into a bank has to either trudge to the last mile to the bank branch to take out their money or wait for an itinerant banking correspondent to come by; banks are engaged in strengthening the network of banking correspondents by creating a registry of banking correspondents, with the ability to take and give cash on behalf of any bank through the Aadhaar Enabled Payment System (which will also give them adequate remuneration), and requiring that they are adequately trained in providing financial services; on 16 October 2022 the Prime Minister launched seventy-five digital Banking Units (DBUs) in seventy-five districts across the country with the objective to promote financial inclusion; DBUs are brick-and-mortar outlets offering a variety of banking facilities such as opening savings bank accounts, investment in term deposits, funds transfer, tax and bill payments; the postal payments bank and telecom affiliated payment banks make post offices and telecom kiosks entry points into the financial system; transfers from bank account to bank account via mobile through the Unified Payments Interface (UPI); small businesses can use the services of an on-line internet platform to sell, creating a verifiable record of revenues that can form the basis for credit (full-service entities that help the small business with marketing and logistics while tying up with a finance company to provide the business with credit); peer-to-peer lending platforms with light-touch regulation.

Some issues and possible resolution (courseware): impediments the excluded could face relate to Know Your Customer requirements; secondly, there is need to promote and encourage competition to prevent exploitation; thirdly, there is need to ensure some flexibility and forgiveness in financial arrangements; fourthly, the need for skilling and support; and finally financial literacy and ensuring consumer protection. Know Your Customer: the RBI has steadily eased the required documentation for basic financial services; for instance recognising that proof of address is difficult, especially for those moving location, RBI requires only one document showing permanent address be presented; current address can be self-certified; going forward the Indian Banks Association could devise common account forms, where minimum RBI requirements will be printed on the back of the form; a basic account (small accounts) can be obtained with some restrictions on amounts and transactions. Competition to prevent exploitation: the excluded are typically risky and exposed to exploitation because they have so little access; exploitation may come from a moneylender who charges usurious rates or a banker demanding gratuity for giving a government-subsidised loan; the fundamental way to deal with exploitation is to increase competition amongst providers of financial services; regulation can help, but we should be careful that regulation does not shut out competition, thus enhancing exploitation (Dr Raghuram Rajan): (i) politicians are rightfully concerned about the poor being charged usurious rates and so often set interest rate ceilings; a clever regulated lender can avoid interest rate ceilings through hidden and not-so-hidden fees; if the ceiling is set too low the regulated lender will not bother to lend since it is not worth his while, so the poor borrower is left to the tender mercies of the rapacious unregulated moneylender; the RBI has been following the Goldilocks principle in setting interest rate ceilings for micro finance firms; (ii) similarly the prohibition on taking collateral up to a certain size to certain borrowers such as students or small businesses may increase access; one reasonable compromise is to allow only unsecured or collateral-free loans to qualify for priority sector treatment or interest subventions, but to also allow institutions to take collateral if offered on ordinary loans, provided they have a policy of charging lower rates on such secured loans. Flexibility and forgiveness: the biggest component of interest costs is the credit risk margin, not the real policy rate; the credit risk margin can be brought down by focusing on improving the lending institutional framework; the RBI guidelines on natural calamities allow banks to need based restructuring of the agricultural loans without classifying them NPA provided there are widespread crop losses; an optional moratorium period during unemployment; individuals including farmers should be allowed bankruptcy, and being relieved of their debts provided this remedy is used sparingly. Skilling and support: a widely perpetuated myth that access to financial services is all that is necessary to set poor farm worker on their path to riches; to generate income in a sustainable way, she needs help in acquiring skills to raise chickens or cows or grow flowers, in marketing, in learning how to manage funds; the Jivika rural livelihoods programme in Bihar; the Government Skill India programme. Financial literacy and consumer protection: the excluded are drawn into formal financial services and will encounter aggressive selling, mis-selling; the RBI has planned a nationwide campaign; RBI has been encouraging financial education to be included in the school curriculum; in June 2012 RBI advised banks to set up Financial Literacy Centres (FLC) in all the districts of the country; banks are advised to scale up financial literacy efforts through outdoor Financial Literacy Camps at least once a month, both by the FLCs and by all the rural branches; in 2015 RBI came out with 5 principles that banks have to follow in dealing with customers (Charter of Consumer Rights); banks are required to appoint an internal ombudsman to monitor the grievance redressal process; the Integrated Ombudsman scheme put in place recently takes note of these requirements.

Financial inclusion progress and plans (courseware): financial inclusion acts as a driver of balanced economic growth. The IMF Financial Access Survey highlights the progress made in dealing with the last mile problem and the increasing popularity of financial products; the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) and its linkage with Aadhaar and mobile phones created the Jan Dhan Yojana, Aadhaar, Mobile (JAM) trinity, which has been a game changer for the welfare schemes under direct benefit transfers (DBTs) as well as for financial inclusion. The National Strategy for Financial Inclusion (NSFI) 2019-2024 and the National Strategy for Financial Education 2020-2025 were released by the Reserve Bank in January 2020 and 2020 respectively. The Reserve Bank introduced the Financial Inclusion Index (FI Index) in August 2021 to monitor progress of policy initiatives to promote financial inclusion; the FI Index is based on 97 indicators representing access, usage and quality; it takes values from 0 to 100; the courseware reports values of 49.9 at March 2019, 53.1 at March 2020 and 53.9 at March 2021. Two distinct pillars of financial inclusion progress in India: (a) advancement in digital technology (FinTech); and (b) greater participation of women; financial inclusion acts as a key facilitator for reducing gender inequality and furthering women empowerment. Financial Inclusion Plans (FIPs) were introduced by the Reserve Bank in 2010 with the objective of encouraging banks to adopt a planned and structured approach towards financial inclusion. Business Facilitators and Business Correspondents: RBI initiated measures to enable banks to use the services of Non-Governmental Organisations / Self Help Groups (NGOs / SHGs), Micro Finance Institutions (MFIs) and other Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) as intermediaries, in providing financial and banking services, through the use of Business Facilitator and Correspondent models. Business Facilitator Model: eligible entities include NGOs, Farmers Clubs, co-operatives, community-based organisations, IT enabled rural outlets of corporate entities, Post Offices, insurance agents, well-functioning Panchayats, Village Knowledge Centres, Agri Clinics / Agri Business Centres, Krishi Vigyan Kendras and KVIC / KVIB units; services include identification of borrowers and fitment of activities, collection and preliminary processing of loan applications including verification of primary information / data, creating awareness about savings and other products and education and advice on managing money and debt counselling, processing and submission of applications to banks, promotion and nurturing of Self-Help Groups / Joint Liability Groups, post-sanction monitoring, monitoring and handholding of SHG / JLGs and follow up for recovery; as these services are not intended to involve the conduct of banking business by Business Facilitators, no approval is required from RBI for using the above intermediaries. Business Correspondent Model: NGOs / MFIs set up under Societies / Trust Acts, Societies registered under Mutually Aided Cooperative Societies Acts or the Cooperative Societies Acts of States, Section 25 companies, registered NBFCs not accepting public deposits and Post Offices may act as Business Correspondents; banks should ensure that they are well established, enjoying good reputation and confidence of the local people; in addition to the Business Facilitator services the BC scope includes: disbursal of small value credit, recovery of principal / collection of interest, collection of small value deposits, sale of micro insurance / mutual fund products / pension products and other third-party products, and receipt and delivery of small value remittances / other payment instruments; the activities are within the normal course of the bank banking business but conducted through the entities at places other than the bank premises; RBI guidelines advise on: formulation of a policy with Board approval, the individuals or entities that can be engaged as BCs, how BCs attached to banks, scope of functioning, KYC / AML, protection of customer information, commission / fee payable to BCs, engagement of BC / BF as an intermediary involves reputational, legal and operational risks so due diligence, a detailed review of the performance of various BCs at least once in a year, and a grievance redressal machinery. By March 2021, BC outlets constituted more than 95 per cent of the total banking outlets in villages (the courseware says that at end-March 2021 BC outlets constituted more than 95 per cent of total banking outlets in villages, with the rapid growth in the number of BCs in villages with population below 2,000). PMJDY: since inception in August 2014 contributing towards financial inclusion of the unserved and underserved population; as on December 15, 2021, the number of total beneficiaries under PMJDY expanded to 44.12 crores, with deposits of Rs 1.49 lakh crore; many accounts are maintained with PSBs and RRBs (97 per cent), nearly two thirds of the total accounts operational in rural and semi-urban areas; the usage of these accounts has been steadily increasing (RuPay debit cards issued); 24.54 crore accounts were opened for women beneficiaries under PMJDY, accounting for 55.6 per cent of total account holders under the scheme. Financial Literacy Centres: as at end December 2021 there were 1,495 financial literacy centres (FLCs) in the country and 73,900 financial literacy activities were conducted during 2021-22 (up to December 31, 2021). Financial inclusion and monetary policy (6.8.4-6.8.7): financial inclusion and monetary policy symbiosis: assimilating the received wisdom and empirical evidence that has been accumulated so far on the subject; drawing applicable lessons from financial inclusion; the Reserve Bank crafted a pandemic response; food inflation has been volatile; financial inclusion appears to have gone up (index rising 49.9 to 53.1 to 53.9); modern central banks mostly employ the interest rate to convey the stance of monetary policy; policy rate changes immediately influence short-term money market rates which affect the continuum of financial markets to longer-term interest rates; financial inclusion improves the transmission of interest-rate-based monetary policy impulses in two ways: (i) the financially excluded would typically prefer inside the pillow savings and for this, cash is the preferred instrument; as inclusion increases, their preference shifts from cash to interest-bearing bank deposits and other financial instruments, so the interest rate sensitivity of money balances also goes up; (ii) financial inclusion is expected to expand the access to bank credit, which is interest sensitive and affected by changes in the policy rate; all in all, financial inclusion enhances the potency of interest-rate-based monetary policy by causing an increasing number of people to become responsive to interest rate cycles; the JAM trinity is widely regarded as having completed inclusion on the deposit side; NABARD self-help group bank linkage programme is the world largest microfinance programme in terms of number of beneficiaries and microcredit extended; RBI Kehta Hai and Interactive Voice Response System (IVRS) are public awareness campaigns for financial literacy.

payload.title: Objectives of financial inclusion and the impediments (IIT)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Three objectives:** **broaden** services to people and firms **with no access**; **deepen** services for those with **minimal access**; and improve **financial literacy and consumer protection** so people **choose appropriately**.

**Why it matters:** it is a policy goal in **over 60 countries**, central to the **UN 2030 SDGs**, supports **stable financial systems** (the **UNCDF** finds the included **ride out interest rate cycles** without being hurt **counter-cyclically**) and **strengthens monetary policy transmission**. In India growth since independence left many outside **formal finance**.

**Impediments (Raghuram Rajan's IIT):**

| Letter | Impediment |
| --- | --- |
| **I - Information** | The excluded work **informally**, keep **no records**, own **little property**: lenders cannot judge **creditworthiness** |
| **I - Incentives** | Lenders avoid them when **repayment cannot be enforced** quickly or cheaply and there is **no collateral** |
| **T - Transaction costs** | **Fixed costs** are high relative to **tiny loan sizes** (the same effort for a **Rs 10,000** loan as for **Rs 10 lakh**) |

Excluded people may also live **remotely** and lack **institutional arrangements** that reward those who serve them.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Rajan's three letters explain why small, informal borrowers are costly for banks to serve.

self_check.prompt_text: What does IIT stand for in Raghuram Rajan's characterisation of the impediments to financial inclusion?

payload.title: Mandates and subventions
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Tools:** **priority sector lending targets**, **opening 25 per cent of branches in unbanked areas**, **interest subventions** and drives such as **PMJDY accounts** and **Mudra loans**.

**Case for mandates:** inclusion has **positive externalities** that the provider cannot capture (the **social status** a worker gains from her **poultry farm** may exceed the bank's cost) and **network benefits** (**direct benefit transfers** and **UPI** work better when **nearly everyone has an account**).

**Risks:** **no market test** of usefulness, **vested interests** keep mandates **alive**, banks **target the easiest eligible borrowers** and **mislabel** normal lending, and **public sector banks** bear most of the burden, which **hurts their profitability**.

**RBI refinements:** revised the **priority sector list** to target the **truly excluded**; **large loans to agri-product firms no longer qualify**; targets are met **every quarter** (limiting **window dressing**); **Priority Sector Lending Certificates** let banks **sell over-achievement**; the courseware says **explicit subsidies** are better than **hidden cross-subsidies** (for example **cash recyclers in underserved areas**). **Mandates are not costless**: cost should be **brought into the open**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Mandates work best when targeted and paid for openly.

self_check.prompt_text: What do Priority Sector Lending Certificates allow a bank to do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Sell over-achievement in a category to banks that are deficient in it.

payload.title: Institutions, digital technology, credit information and payments
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Why local institutions:** moneylenders succeed through **local knowledge**; **large bank managers** are often **outsiders** and **centralised**; **HDFC Bank** grew in **Kashmir** by hiring **local loan officers**; **MFIs** use **peer pressure and frequent repayment**. **Limits:** MFIs lack **low-cost deposits**; **local area banks** face **geographical concentration**; **RRBs** are costly and **co-operative banks** suffer **governance weaknesses** with **split supervision**.

**Small finance banks:** 'small' refers to the **customer**; **75 per cent of loans to the priority sector** and **50 per cent of the portfolio in loans below Rs 25 lakh**.

**Information tools:** **credit information bureaus** (**CIBIL**, one free report a year); bringing **SHG borrowing** into their ambit; **Aadhaar** for identity; **Udyog Aadhaar** for small firms; **digitised land records** (a **Rajasthan** proposal) to make **land usable as collateral**; **TReDS** platforms let **MSMEs** sell claims on **large buyers** instead of waiting for late payments.

**Payments before credit:** encourage **savings** and let **credit follow** (as **SHGs** do). Easy **cash in and out** needs **banking correspondents** (a **registry**, **Aadhaar Enabled Payment System**, training, pay), **post office and telecom payments banks**, **UPI** (a **mobile number or alias** is enough), and **75 digital banking units** launched on **16 October 2022**. Small businesses can build **verifiable revenue records** on **online platforms**, and **peer-to-peer lending** under **light-touch regulation** may help.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Local knowledge, data and easy payments replace the moneylender's information advantage.

self_check.prompt_text: What does TReDS help an MSME do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Sell its claim on a large buyer in the market instead of waiting for late payment.

payload.title: Issues in financial inclusion and their resolution
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Five issues:** **KYC**, **competition and exploitation**, **flexibility and forgiveness**, **skilling and support**, **financial literacy and consumer protection**.

- **KYC:** the Reserve Bank has **eased documentation**: **one document for permanent address**, **self-certified current address**, **basic (small) accounts** with limits; the **Indian Banks' Association** could use **common account forms**.
- **Competition:** exploitation comes from **moneylenders and corrupt bankers**; **competition** is the main protection. **Interest rate ceilings** can backfire (**hidden fees**, or lenders **stop lending**): the Reserve Bank follows the **Goldilocks principle** for micro finance. **Collateral bans** can also **cut access**; a compromise is **collateral-free loans for priority sector status** while letting banks **charge lower rates on secured loans**.
- **Flexibility and forgiveness:** the biggest part of interest cost is the **credit risk margin**; fix the **lending framework** and allow **restructuring of agricultural loans after natural calamities without NPA classification**, **moratoria** during unemployment and **personal bankruptcy** used sparingly.
- **Skilling and support:** access alone does not lift the poor; they need **skills, marketing and money management** (**Jivika** in Bihar, **Skill India**).
- **Literacy and protection:** guard against **aggressive selling and mis-selling**; **Financial Literacy Centres** in all districts (**June 2012**) holding **monthly camps**; the **2015 Charter of Consumer Rights** (five principles); an **internal ombudsman** in banks; the **Integrated Ombudsman Scheme** strengthens redress.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Inclusion needs documentation relief, competition, forgiveness, skills and protection together.

self_check.prompt_text: What principle does the Reserve Bank follow in setting interest rate ceilings for micro finance firms, as described in this unit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Goldilocks principle: neither too high nor too low.

payload.title: Progress, business correspondents and the link with monetary policy
payload.core_explanation_md:
**JAM trinity:** **Jan Dhan Yojana + Aadhaar + Mobile**, a **game changer** for **direct benefit transfers**; **PMJDY** began in **August 2014** (**97 per cent** of accounts in PSBs and RRBs, women about **55.6 per cent**).

**Strategies and indices:** the **National Strategy for Financial Inclusion 2019-2024** and the **National Strategy for Financial Education 2020-2025**; the **Financial Inclusion Index (August 2021)**: **97 indicators** across **access, usage and quality**, scored **0 to 100**.

**Pillars:** **digital technology (FinTech)** and **women's participation**. **Financial Inclusion Plans** were introduced in **2010** to push banks to a **planned approach**.

**Intermediaries:**

| Model | Allowed entities | Activities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Business Facilitator** | NGOs, farmers' clubs, co-operatives, **post offices**, **insurance agents**, Panchayats, **Krishi Vigyan Kendras** and others | **Identify borrowers**, **process loan applications**, **awareness and counselling**, **promote SHGs/JLGs**, **monitor and follow up** (no RBI approval needed; **not banking business**) |
| **Business Correspondent** | **NGOs/MFIs**, **Section 25 companies**, **NBFCs not taking deposits**, **post offices**, societies | All BF services plus **small credit disbursal**, **recovery**, **small deposits**, **micro insurance/mutual fund/pension sales** and **remittances**; banks need a **Board policy**, **KYC/AML**, **due diligence**, an **annual review** and **grievance redress** |

BCs supply **more than 95 per cent of banking outlets in villages** (**March 2021**).

**Monetary policy link:** inclusion **improves interest-rate transmission**: the excluded keep **cash under the pillow** (not interest-sensitive); as they join, savings shift to **interest-bearing deposits** and **credit** (interest-sensitive) grows, so **policy rate changes reach more people**. **NABARD's SHG-bank linkage** is the **world's largest microfinance programme**; **RBI Kehta Hai** and **IVRS** spread literacy.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: More people holding deposits and loans means more households respond to interest rate signals.

self_check.prompt_text: How does financial inclusion strengthen monetary policy transmission?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It moves people from cash to interest-bearing deposits and credit, making more households sensitive to policy rate changes.
